name: Yellowstone: Geyser Country
description: Madison Junction to Craig Pass along the Grand Loop Road, through the Lower, Midway and Upper Geyser Basins.
note: Coordinates are approximate and intended for a demo. Verify against official NPS data before relying on them.

intro.title: Welcome to Yellowstone
intro.story: Welcome to Yellowstone, the world's first national park, established on March 1, 1872. You are driving across one of the largest active volcanic systems on Earth. The heat from below powers more than ten thousand hydrothermal features, including roughly half of the world's active geysers. Sit back and keep your eyes on the road, and I'll tell you about the places you pass.

pois.name: Madison Junction
pois.story: Right here, the Gibbon and Firehole rivers meet to form the Madison River, one of the three rivers that join to form the Missouri. Lewis and Clark named the Madison in 1805 after James Madison, who was Secretary of State at the time. The peak above the junction is called National Park Mountain. Legend says that in September 1870, members of the Washburn expedition sat around a campfire nearby and came up with the idea of protecting this land as a national park. Historians now think the campfire story was embellished later, but it was so popular that it gave the mountain its name.

pois.name: Firehole Canyon
pois.story: The cliffs on your right are layers of rhyolite, lava that flowed across this area after Yellowstone's last great eruption. The Firehole River has cut a canyon straight through them. The name comes from early fur trappers, who used the word 'hole' for a mountain valley and thought the steam rising from the geyser basins upstream looked like smoke from a fire. A short one-way side road, Firehole Canyon Drive, leads past the forty-foot Firehole Falls.

pois.name: Nez Perce Creek
pois.story: This creek is named for the Nez Perce people. In August 1877, roughly eight hundred Nez Perce men, women and children, pursued by the U.S. Army, crossed Yellowstone as they fled toward Canada. They came up this valley from the Lower Geyser Basin. Along the way they met parties of tourists in the park, which was only five years old at the time. The Nez Perce eventually surrendered in Montana that October, about forty miles from the Canadian border.

pois.name: Fountain Paint Pot
pois.story: Coming up is Fountain Paint Pot, one of the few places where a short boardwalk shows you all four types of Yellowstone's hydrothermal features: hot springs, geysers, fumaroles, and mudpots. The mudpots form where acidic gases break down the surrounding rock into clay. In the wet spring the mud is thin and splashy, and by late summer it thickens into a bubbling paste. Nearby Clepsydra Geyser has been erupting almost nonstop since the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake.

pois.name: Grand Prismatic Spring
pois.story: Look to your right for steam drifting over the Midway Geyser Basin. It's home to Grand Prismatic Spring, the largest hot spring in the United States and the third largest in the world, about three hundred seventy feet across. The rainbow colors come from microbial mats, communities of heat-loving microorganisms. Each color band lives at a different temperature. The deep blue center is too hot for most life and gets its color from the way water scatters light. Next to it is the huge crater of Excelsior Geyser, which pours thousands of gallons of hot water into the Firehole River every minute.

pois.name: Biscuit Basin
pois.story: Biscuit Basin is named for knobby mineral deposits that once surrounded Sapphire Pool and looked like biscuits. After the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake, Sapphire Pool erupted violently and blew most of the biscuits away. The basin is still changing. In July 2024, a hydrothermal explosion near Black Diamond Pool threw rocks and debris into the air and wrecked part of the boardwalk. It's a reminder that the ground here is alive.

pois.name: Black Sand Basin
pois.story: Black Sand Basin gets its name from sand made of obsidian, a black volcanic glass. Look for Emerald Pool, where yellow microbes on a blue background make the water glow green. Early visitors loved Handkerchief Pool, where a dropped handkerchief would be pulled under and pop back up clean a few moments later. Sadly, the debris people threw in later clogged it, a lesson in why we stay on the boardwalk and never toss anything into a thermal feature.

pois.name: Upper Geyser Basin
pois.story: You are now entering the Upper Geyser Basin, home to the largest concentration of geysers anywhere on Earth. About one hundred fifty geysers are packed into roughly one square mile. Besides Old Faithful, the basin includes giants like Grand Geyser, the tallest geyser that is regularly predicted, and Castle Geyser, whose cone may be thousands of years old.

pois.name: Old Faithful
pois.story: Up ahead is Old Faithful, named in 1870 by the Washburn expedition for its reliable eruptions. It isn't the tallest or the most regular geyser in the park, but it's the most famous. It erupts about every sixty to one hundred ten minutes, sending water between one hundred and one hundred eighty-five feet into the air. Rangers predict the next eruption from the length of the last one, since a longer eruption means a longer wait. Check the prediction board at the visitor center to see when the next show starts.

pois.name: Kepler Cascades
pois.story: Kepler Cascades is a series of drops on the Firehole River totaling about one hundred fifty feet, and there's a viewing platform right next to the road. In 1881, park superintendent Philetus Norris named the cascades after Kepler Hoyt, the twelve-year-old son of Wyoming's territorial governor, who was touring the park with his father.

pois.name: Isa Lake at Craig Pass
pois.story: You're crossing the Continental Divide at Craig Pass. The small lily-covered pond beside the road is Isa Lake, and it drains into both oceans. Because the Divide loops around here, the water that leaves the east side of the lake ends up in the Pacific, and the water that leaves the west side reaches the Atlantic by way of the Missouri and Mississippi. That's the opposite of what you'd expect.

ambient.title: Yellowstone's bison
ambient.story: Yellowstone is the only place in the United States where bison have lived continuously since prehistoric times. If you meet them on the road, stay in your car and let them pass. Park rules ask you to stay at least twenty-five yards from bison and elk, and one hundred yards from bears and wolves.

ambient.title: A microbe that changed medicine
ambient.story: In 1966, microbiologist Thomas Brock found a heat-loving bacterium, Thermus aquaticus, living in a Yellowstone hot spring. An enzyme from it, Taq polymerase, later made the PCR technique practical. PCR is used everywhere today, from DNA fingerprinting to medical testing.

ambient.title: Driving through a caldera
ambient.story: Much of this drive runs inside the Yellowstone Caldera, a huge volcanic depression left by an eruption roughly six hundred thirty thousand years ago. It's so large that it's hard to see from the ground. The rhyolite lava flows that later filled it make up the plateaus and cliffs around you.

ambient.title: The fires of 1988
ambient.story: In the summer of 1988, wildfires burned about a third of Yellowstone. The young lodgepole pines you see growing thickly along the road sprouted after those fires. Many lodgepoles have cones sealed with resin that only open in intense heat, so fire helps plant the next forest.

ambient.title: The return of the wolves
ambient.story: Gray wolves had been wiped out of Yellowstone by the 1920s. They were brought back in 1995 and 1996, and today they are one of the best-studied wolf populations in the world. Their return affected elk behavior and set off ripple effects that scientists are still debating.
